0508-value.title: Assessed Value of Household and Kitchen Furniture Owned by Georgia Negroes.
0508-value.caption: Assessed Value of Household and Kitchen Furniture Owned by Georgia Negroes.
0508-value.creditLine: Image courtesy of the Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, LC-DIG-ppmsca-33887.
0508-value.digitizedLine: Digitized by the Library of Congress.
0508-value.altText: A bar chart where six curving bars of color spiral toward the center of the page to indicate the value of household and kitchen furniture owned by Black Georgians from 1875 to 1899. The colors are all aligned in a row at the top of the page from 1875 to 1899, and each color corresponds to a year and value dollar amount. The topmost bar for 1875 is pink and is the smallest curving line, just barely beginning to curve, with the value of household furniture coming to $21,186. A blue curving bar falls just under the pink to represent 1880’s value of kitchen and household furniture, reaching $498,532. The next curving bar is brown for the year 1885 with a value of Black-owned furniture in Georgia reaching $736,170. Beneath the brown bar is a yellow curving bar for 1890, for which $1,173,624 was assessed to be the value of household and kitchen items owned by Black Georgians. The second bottom-most curving light gray bar shows that the value for Black-owned furniture in 1895 was $1,322,694. The last curving bar is red for the year 1899 and indicates that the value of household and kitchen furniture owned by Black Georgians reached $1,434,975. Each curving bar grows a bit longer than the previous bar, demonstrating the increasing value of furniture Black Georgians owned in the twenty-five years leading up to the Paris Exposition.

0510-illiteracy.title: Illiteracy.
0510-illiteracy.caption: Illiteracy.
0510-illiteracy.creditLine: Image courtesy of the Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, LC-DIG-ppmsca-33876.
0510-illiteracy.digitizedLine: Digitized by the Library of Congress.
0510-illiteracy.altText: A bar diagram of interweaving perpendicular and parallel bars that tracks illiteracy percentages of Black Georgians between 1860 and 1900 every ten years. Each year is listed from earliest to latest, top to bottom, and is connected to its corresponding illiteracy percentage by a bar that, when horizontal, is not shaded in and, when vertical, is colored in black. The four bars begin horizontally and turn downward to connect to their respective percentages, creating a criss-cross pattern. The first bar for the year 1860 measures 99 percent illiteracy in the Black Georgian population, so the horizontal portion of the bar does not extend far into the page. The bar for 1870 measures 92 percent illiteracy, thus the horizontal bar stretches farther than the previous year, but not by much. In 1880, the illiteracy percentage decreased to 81.8 percent, and in 1890, the illiteracy percentage decreased to 67.2 percent, both horizontal bars taking up more space than the previous year(s). Lastly, in 1900, the percentage of illiterate Black Georgians decreased once again to 50 percent of the population, the horizontal bar stretching the width of the chart.

0511-master-rbc-rbaapc-10601-0031.altText: Part grid and part area chart, this colorful graphic shows the marital status of Black men and women in the United States according to their age. The horizontal X axis measures the percentage (from 0 to 100%) of men and women who are single, married, or widowed, and the vertical Y axis measures age. The age increments from bottom to top, are listed as follows: 0 to 15; 15 to 20; 20 to 25; 25 to 30; 30 to 35; 35 to 45; 45 to 55; 55 to 65; and over age 65. Divided vertically in the middle, the left side of the grid tracks Black men’s marital status, and the right side measures Black women’s. Green space, which indicates widowers, occupies each top corner and falls vertically, serving as a border to the majority of the other categories; Pink space sits next to the green to show who is married; and Blue lies in the center and along the bottom next to the red area to depict those who are single.

0515-916-amalg.title: The Amalgamation of the White and Black elements of the population in the United States.
0515-916-amalg.caption: The Amalgamation of the White and Black elements of the population in the United States.
0515-916-amalg.creditLine: Image courtesy of the Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, LC-DIG-ppmsca-33916.
0515-916-amalg.digitizedLine: Digitized by the Library of Congress.
0515-916-amalg.altText: A chart that shows the increasing number of Black and Black multiracial residents in the United States from 1800 to 1890. Drawn resembling a steep mountaintop, which begins at 1800 on the right of the page and falls to 1890 at the bottom left, the chart’s downward motion emphasizes how the range and scope of blackness shifted during the nineteenth century. To depict what Du Bois labels as the “amalgamation” of the growing number of Black people in the United States and their shifting phenotypes, the chart sections off three discrete racial categories by hue, which lighten gradually from black to white. The Black population is colored in black and implies that this portion of the population showed no visual trace of interracial coupling. To its right, the color grows slightly lighter as it nears what Du Bois labels as the “mulatto” or multiracial population, which is split between a light brown and a dark yellow color to depict the portion of the Black population that announces a white presence in one’s lineage. The white population section is predominately drawn with the paper’s off-white hue, except for a light yellow gradient where it comes into contact with the multiracial population, to its left. There is no quantitative data associated with the white population. While no percentages or numbers are stated in the slimmer sections tracking the 1800s or 1840s, the chart shows that by 1860 the Black population amounted to 3,542,147 people–90% of all Black people in America–and the multiracial population made up the remaining 10% of the total Black population. In 1890, while both grew in size, the Black population decreased to 85% (6,337,980 people) while the Black multiracial population increased to 15% (1,113,063 people).

0516-master-pnp-ppmsca-08700-08778u.title: [Four African American women seated on steps of building at Atlanta University, Georgia]
0516-master-pnp-ppmsca-08700-08778u.caption: Four Atlanta University women students posed on the steps of a classroom building, photographed by Thomas Askew for the Paris Exposition.
0516-master-pnp-ppmsca-08700-08778u.creditLine: Image courtesy of the Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division, LC-DIG-ppmsca-08778.
0516-master-pnp-ppmsca-08700-08778u.digitizedLine: Digitized by the Library of Congress.
0516-master-pnp-ppmsca-08700-08778u.altText: Four Black women clad in skirts, button-down, high-collared shirts, and hats sit on steps outside. 0519-chalabi-illiteracy.title: Illiteracy
0519-chalabi-illiteracy.caption: Du Bois's chart of "Illiteracy" recreated with contemporary data by Mona Chalabi.
0519-chalabi-illiteracy.creditLine: Photo by Mona Chalabi. Image courtesy of Mona Chalabi.
0519-chalabi-illiteracy.notes: Mona granted permission. Have high res versions too.
0519-chalabi-illiteracy.altText: Two bar diagrams (one recreation on the right of the original left image) of interweaving perpendicular and parallel bars that tracks illiteracy percentages of Black Georgians between 1860 and 1900 every ten years. Each year is listed from earliest to latest, top to bottom, and is connected to its corresponding illiteracy percentage by a bar that, when horizontal, is not shaded in and, when vertical, is colored in black. The four bars begin horizontally and turn downward to connect to their respective percentages, creating a criss-cross pattern. The first bar for the year 1860 measures 99 percent illiteracy in the Black Georgian population, so the horizontal portion of the bar does not extend far into the page. The bar for 1870 measures 92 percent illiteracy, thus the horizontal bar stretches farther than the previous year, but not by much. In 1880, the illiteracy percentage decreased to 81.8 percent, and in 1890, the illiteracy percentage decreased to 67.2 percent, both horizontal bars taking up more space than the previous year(s). Lastly, in 1900, the percentage of illiterate Black Georgians decreased once again to 50 percent of the population, the horizontal bar stretching the width of the chart. The recreation on the right also adds the 2010 statistics for illiteracy, where the white fragment of the bar stretches far across the page compared to the above bars, to show 2 percent illiteracy.

0520-chalabi-worth.title: Net Worth of Households
0520-chalabi-worth.caption: Du Bois's chart of household possessions recreated with contemporary data by Mona Chalabi.
0520-chalabi-worth.creditLine: Photo by Mona Chalabi. Image courtesy of Mona Chalabi.
0520-chalabi-worth.notes: Mona granted permission. Have high res versions too.
0520-chalabi-worth.altText: Two bar charts side by side. On the left chart, six curving bars of color spiral toward the center of the page to indicate the value of household and kitchen furniture owned by Black Georgians from 1875 to 1899. The colors are all aligned in a row at the top of the page from 1875 to 1899, and each color corresponds to a year and value dollar amount. The topmost bar for 1875 is pink and is the smallest curving line, just barely beginning to curve, with the value of household furniture coming to $21,186. A blue curving bar falls just under the pink to represent 1880’s value of kitchen and household furniture, reaching $498,532. The next curving bar is brown for the year 1885 with a value of Black-owned furniture in Georgia reaching $736,170. Beneath the brown bar is a yellow curving bar for 1890, for which $1,173,624 was assessed to be the value of household and kitchen items owned by Black Georgians. The second bottom-most curving light gray bar shows that the value for Black-owned furniture in 1895 was $1,322,694. The last curving bar is red for the year 1899 and indicates that the value of household and kitchen furniture owned by Black Georgians reached $1,434,975. Each curving bar grows a bit longer than the previous bar, demonstrating the increasing value of furniture Black Georgians owned in the twenty-five years leading up to the Paris Exposition. The right chart recreates the imagery of the original left but instead measures “Net Worth of Households” according to racial group. According to the chart, Black households (represented in light blue) are worth $6,314, Hispanic households (represented in brown) are worth $7,683, the households of other races not specifically named (represented in yellow) are worth $19,023, Asian households (represented in gray) are worth $89,339, and white households (represented in red) are worth $110,500.

0525-899-series.title: A series of statistical charts illustrating the condition of the descendants of former African slaves now in residence in the United States of America
0525-899-series.caption: The title image of the second set of charts prepared for the Paris Exposition, “A Series of Statistical Charts Illustrating the Condition of the Descendants of Former African Slaves Now Resident in the United States of America.”
0525-899-series.creditLine: Image courtesy of the Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, LC-DIG-ppmsca-08994.
0525-899-series.digitizedLine: Digitized by the Library of Congress.
0525-899-series.altText: The first chart in the second series presented at the Paris Exposition is dense with text in both English and French to highlight the history and role of Atlanta University students–and the institution itself–in creating the data portraits. The text describes the year the college was founded (1867), the total number of Black students who have attended the university (6,000 at the time of the study), and the total number of graduates from the university (330 students) who have since gone on to work in various fields described in a pie chart. The multicolor pie chart sits in the middle of the page describing employment and other conditions of Black Americans with a key in English to the left and in French to the right of the chart. The largest section of the pie chart is colored in red and records that 58.5 percent of the Black American population works as teachers. The second largest portion of the chart is yellow and shows 28.1 percent of the population is designated as house wives. Decreasing substantially in size to 4.3 percent is the next population of Black American employees who work as ministers, indicated in blue. Other professions and government service follow at 3.8 and 3.2 percent respectively, with other professions colored in green and government service in pink. The smallest portion of Black American employment is under the category of business, which is shaded in light brown and is recorded at 2.1 percent. A small multicolored map of the United States also rests under the title of the piece with a star over Atlanta, GA to indicate the center of the Black population in the country. More text at the bottom of the page states the number of current Black professors, faculty, and students at Atlanta University at the time of the study (20 professors and faculty; 250 students), along with a description of the size of the campus (60 acres) and number of buildings (5), including the library which holds 11,000 volumes. Lastly, the text describes the university’s endowment of $500,000 and the mission of the university, which is “to raise and civilize the songs of the freedmen by training their more capable members in the liberal arts according to the best standards of the day.”
